text:
Dear Dr. Henderson,

Thank you for agreeing to see this 20-year-old male university student who presents for evaluation of long-standing, progressive weakness. His difficulties date back to early childhood with generalized lack of stamina and repeated falls, although his early motor milestones were met on schedule. 

On physical examination, he appears thin with diffuse muscle wasting, though no enlarged muscle groups or pseudohypertrophy are visible. Cranial examination reveals an elongated facial morphology, a notably high-arched roof of the mouth, and a small, retrognathic mandible. There is no eyelid drooping, and he denies double vision. Speech is fluent and clear, and swallowing is preserved. He has marked weakness when flexing his neck against resistance. Musculoskeletal evaluation shows straight spinal alignment without lateral curvature, but his shoulder blades wing prominently from the thoracic wall. Lower limb examination demonstrates flat feet with significant hindfoot valgus deviation. Reflex testing reveals a complete absence of all deep tendon reflexes. Sensory examination is unremarkable, with intact perception of light touch and vibration distally.

The patient remains able to walk independently, though he ambulates with a pronounced pelvic waddle. He is comfortably able to walk on his tiptoes and heels. He reports no muscle pain or cramps, has no history of tea-colored urine, and has had no recurrent chest infections. 

Recent workup revealed a normal serum creatine kinase. Motor nerve conduction velocities were within normal limits throughout. However, magnetic resonance imaging of his legs demonstrated extensive fibrofatty infiltration replacing normal skeletal muscle architecture. 

He takes only an over-the-counter multivitamin, and his family history is entirely negative for neurological disease. I would appreciate your expert opinion regarding his presentation and recommendations for diagnostic management.

Sincerely,

Dr. Arthur Vance
